description: Question bank derived from Agricultural Science Comprehensive Objective Q&A Study Material for FDA & SDA competitive examination preparation. Verify current scheme values from official portals.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is agriculture?

options.A: Only the cultivation of soil and growing of crops
options.B: The science, art and business of cultivating soil, growing crops and rearing livestock, including allied activities
options.C: Only the rearing of livestock for milk and meat
options.D: Only the marketing of farm produce

questions.explanation: Agriculture includes crop cultivation, livestock rearing and allied activities such as horticulture, forestry, fisheries and sericulture.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which of the following is included in the scope of agriculture?

options.A: Crop production and soil science only
options.B: Plant breeding and plant protection only
options.C: Crop production, soil science, plant breeding, plant protection, irrigation, animal husbandry, fisheries, agricultural economics, extension, storage and marketing
options.D: Only irrigation and agricultural engineering

questions.explanation: The scope of agriculture spans crop production through storage and marketing, including animal husbandry and fisheries.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is subsistence farming?

options.A: Farming mainly for sale in markets with high productivity
options.B: Farming mainly to produce food and necessities for the farmer's household with little surplus for sale
options.C: Farming using high inputs per unit of land
options.D: Farming over large areas with low inputs

questions.explanation: Subsistence farming produces mainly for the household with relatively little surplus for sale.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is commercial farming?

options.A: Farming only for household consumption
options.B: Farming primarily for sale in markets, focusing on income, productivity and market demand
options.C: Farming without any irrigation
options.D: Farming that prohibits synthetic inputs

questions.explanation: Commercial farming is market-oriented and focuses on income and productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is intensive farming?

options.A: A system using low inputs per unit of land over large areas
options.B: A system using high inputs of labour, capital, fertilisers, irrigation or technology per unit of land to obtain high output per unit area
options.C: A system combining crops with livestock only
options.D: A system dependent only on rainfall

questions.explanation: Intensive farming applies high inputs per unit area for high output per unit area.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is extensive farming?

options.A: A system using high inputs per unit of land
options.B: A system using relatively low inputs per unit of land, generally over large areas, with often lower output per hectare
options.C: A system growing two crops together in rows
options.D: A system restricted to organic inputs

questions.explanation: Extensive farming uses low inputs per unit land over large areas; output per hectare is often lower than intensive systems.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is mixed farming?

options.A: Growing two or more crops together without row arrangement
options.B: A farming system combining crop cultivation with livestock rearing, allowing use of crop residues and animal manure together
options.C: Farming only in dryland areas
options.D: Farming using only organic inputs

questions.explanation: Mixed farming combines crops and livestock so that residues and manure are used together.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is organic farming?

options.A: A production system that uses only chemical fertilisers
options.B: A production system emphasising ecological processes, biodiversity and nutrient cycling while restricting or prohibiting specified synthetic inputs under applicable standards
options.C: Farming without any pest control
options.D: Farming only in greenhouses

questions.explanation: Organic farming emphasises ecological processes and restricts or prohibits specified synthetic inputs under standards.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Does organic farming mean no pest control or fertiliser use?

options.A: Yes, organic farming prohibits all pest control
options.B: No, it uses permitted inputs and ecological methods such as compost, crop rotation, biological control and approved organic amendments
options.C: Yes, no fertiliser of any kind is used
options.D: No, but only synthetic pesticides may be used

questions.explanation: Organic farming uses permitted inputs and ecological methods; certification rules define what is allowed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is sustainable agriculture?

options.A: Agriculture that maximises yield at any environmental cost
options.B: Agriculture that maintains productivity while conserving soil, water and biodiversity, supporting livelihoods without undermining future production
options.C: Agriculture dependent only on rainfall
options.D: Agriculture using only traditional tools

questions.explanation: Sustainable agriculture balances productivity with conservation of soil, water and biodiversity for future needs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is dryland farming?

options.A: Crop production in areas where rainfall is the main water source and irrigation is absent or limited
options.B: Crop production with assured canal irrigation
options.C: Farming in waterlogged areas
options.D: Farming only in coastal regions

questions.explanation: Dryland farming relies mainly on rainfall with moisture conservation and drought-resilient practices.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is rainfed agriculture?

options.A: Agriculture dependent mainly on rainfall rather than irrigation
options.B: Agriculture using only drip irrigation
options.C: Agriculture using only canal water
options.D: Agriculture using groundwater only

questions.explanation: Rainfed agriculture depends mainly on rainfall and may include both dryland and wetter rainfed systems.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is irrigated farming?

options.A: Crop production depending only on rainfall
options.B: Crop production in which water is deliberately supplied to fields through canals, wells, tanks, pumps or other systems
options.C: Farming without any water supply
options.D: Farming only in greenhouses

questions.explanation: Irrigated farming involves deliberate water supply through canals, wells, tanks, pumps or other systems.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is a cropping pattern?

options.A: The yearly sequence and spatial arrangement of crops grown on a piece of land
options.B: The type of soil in a field
options.C: The method of irrigation used
options.D: The type of livestock kept on a farm

questions.explanation: A cropping pattern is the yearly sequence and spatial arrangement of crops, influenced by climate, soil, water, markets and resources.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is a cropping system?

options.A: Only the crops grown in one season
options.B: The crops and their management practices used on a farm over time, including rotations, sequences, intercropping and associated livestock
options.C: Only the irrigation schedule of a farm
options.D: Only the fertiliser schedule of a farm

questions.explanation: A cropping system includes crops and management practices over time, including rotations, sequences, intercropping and associated livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are India's main agricultural seasons?

options.A: Summer, Winter and Autumn
options.B: Kharif, Rabi and Zaid
options.C: Spring, Monsoon and Harvest
options.D: Pre-monsoon and Post-monsoon only

questions.explanation: Kharif, Rabi and Zaid are the broad seasonal groupings in Indian agriculture; exact periods vary by region.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are Kharif crops?

options.A: Winter crops sown after the monsoon
options.B: Monsoon-season crops generally sown with the onset of the southwest monsoon and harvested around autumn
options.C: Short-duration summer crops between Rabi harvest and Kharif sowing
options.D: Perennial plantation crops only

questions.explanation: Kharif crops are monsoon-season crops such as rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, groundnut and soybean.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which of the following are examples of Kharif crops?

options.A: Wheat, barley, gram and mustard
options.B: Rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, groundnut and soybean
options.C: Watermelon, muskmelon and cucumber only
options.D: Tea, coffee and rubber only

questions.explanation: Kharif examples include rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, groundnut and soybean.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are Rabi crops?

options.A: Monsoon-season crops harvested in autumn
options.B: Winter-season crops generally sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring
options.C: Short-duration summer crops
options.D: Crops grown only in coastal areas

questions.explanation: Rabi crops are winter crops sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring; examples include wheat, barley, gram, mustard and peas.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are examples of Rabi crops?

options.A: Rice, maize and cotton
options.B: Wheat, barley, gram, mustard and peas
options.C: Watermelon, muskmelon and cucumber
options.D: Groundnut, soybean and bajra

questions.explanation: Rabi examples include wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas and some rabi jowar.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are Zaid crops?

options.A: Monsoon-season crops
options.B: Winter-season crops
options.C: Short-duration summer crops grown between the Rabi harvest and Kharif sowing
options.D: Perennial plantation crops

questions.explanation: Zaid crops are short-duration summer crops such as watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, summer pulses and some vegetables.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are examples of Zaid crops?

options.A: Wheat, barley and gram
options.B: Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and summer pulses
options.C: Rice, maize and cotton
options.D: Coffee, tea and rubber

questions.explanation: Zaid crops include watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, summer pulses and some vegetables.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which season is described as the short summer interval between Rabi harvest and Kharif sowing?

options.A: Kharif
options.B: Rabi
options.C: Zaid
options.D: Monsoon

questions.explanation: Zaid is the short summer interval between the Rabi harvest and Kharif sowing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Give a simple comparison of Kharif, Rabi and Zaid seasons.

options.A: Kharif: winter; Rabi: monsoon; Zaid: autumn
options.B: Kharif: monsoon; Rabi: winter; Zaid: short summer interval
options.C: Kharif: summer; Rabi: autumn; Zaid: winter
options.D: Kharif: spring; Rabi: summer; Zaid: winter

questions.explanation: Kharif is monsoon, Rabi is winter and Zaid is the short summer interval; the calendar varies by agro-climatic region.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are the major food crops of India?

options.A: Cotton, sugarcane and jute only
options.B: Rice, wheat, maize, millets, pulses and other cereals
options.C: Tea, coffee and rubber only
options.D: Tobacco and oilseeds only

questions.explanation: Rice, wheat, maize, millets, pulses and other cereals form important parts of India's food-crop production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are major commercial crops of India?

options.A: Rice and wheat only
options.B: Cotton, sugarcane, jute, tea, coffee, rubber, tobacco, oilseeds and several horticultural crops
options.C: Millets and pulses only
options.D: Only fruits and vegetables

questions.explanation: Commercial crops include cotton, sugarcane, jute, tea, coffee, rubber, tobacco, oilseeds and several horticultural crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What are the major crops of Karnataka?

options.A: Only wheat and barley
options.B: Rice, ragi, maize, jowar, pulses, groundnut, sunflower, cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, coconut, arecanut, coffee, spices, fruits and vegetables
options.C: Only tea and rubber
options.D: Only cotton and sugarcane

questions.explanation: Karnataka's major crops include rice, ragi, maize, jowar, pulses, groundnut, sunflower, cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, coconut, arecanut, coffee, spices, fruits and vegetables; the crop mix varies by district.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are associated with the Malnad and coastal regions of Karnataka?

options.A: Wheat, barley and mustard
options.B: Rice, arecanut, coconut, spices and plantation crops, with coffee prominent in parts of the Western Ghats and Malnad
options.C: Cotton, soybean and sunflower only
options.D: Safflower and castor only

questions.explanation: Rice, arecanut, coconut, spices and plantation crops are important in many Malnad and coastal areas, with coffee prominent in parts of the Western Ghats and Malnad.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are important in northern Karnataka?

options.A: Coffee, arecanut and coconut only
options.B: Jowar, pulses, cotton, soybean, groundnut, sunflower and other dryland crops
options.C: Tea, rubber and cardamom only
options.D: Rice and sugarcane only

questions.explanation: Jowar, pulses, cotton, soybean, groundnut, sunflower and other dryland crops are important in many northern districts; local patterns differ with rainfall and irrigation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is a plantation crop?

options.A: A crop grown only in the rainy season
options.B: A crop generally grown on a large scale in estates or plantations, often perennial and commercially marketed
options.C: A crop grown only for household consumption
options.D: A short-duration summer crop

questions.explanation: Plantation crops are generally grown on a large scale in estates, often perennial and commercially marketed; examples include tea, coffee, rubber and coconut.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is a cash crop?

options.A: A crop grown mainly for direct household consumption
options.B: A crop grown primarily for sale rather than direct household consumption
options.C: A crop grown only in Zaid season
options.D: A crop grown only without irrigation

questions.explanation: A cash crop is grown primarily for sale; examples include cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, coffee and some oils.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is food security?

options.A: The ability of a country to export food
options.B: A condition in which all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food meeting dietary needs for an active and healthy life
options.C: The total foodgrain production of a country
options.D: The storage capacity of the Food Corporation of India

questions.explanation: Food security means physical and economic access for all people at all times to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active and healthy life.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: What is agricultural extension?

options.A: The expansion of agricultural land area
options.B: The process of sharing research-based knowledge and skills with farmers and supporting adoption of improved practices through education, demonstrations and advisory services
options.C: The extension of irrigation canals
options.D: The extension of farm credit facilities

questions.explanation: Agricultural extension shares research-based knowledge and skills with farmers and supports adoption through education, demonstrations and advisory services.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are associated with the Kharif season according to the exam-fact table?

options.A: Wheat, barley and gram
options.B: Rice, maize, cotton, groundnut, soybean, jowar and bajra
options.C: Watermelon, muskmelon and cucumber
options.D: Tea, coffee and rubber

questions.explanation: Kharif crops include rice, maize, cotton, groundnut, soybean, jowar and bajra.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are associated with the Rabi season according to the exam-fact table?

options.A: Rice, maize and cotton
options.B: Wheat, barley, gram, mustard and peas
options.C: Watermelon and muskmelon
options.D: Groundnut and soybean

questions.explanation: Rabi crops include wheat, barley, gram, mustard and peas.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Fundamentals of Agriculture
questions.question: Which crops are associated with the Zaid season according to the exam-fact table?

options.A: Wheat, barley and gram
options.B: Rice, maize and cotton
options.C: Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and summer pulses
options.D: Coffee, tea and rubber

questions.explanation: Zaid crops include watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and summer pulses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil?

options.A: Only broken rock particles
options.B: A dynamic natural body consisting of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms, supporting plant growth and ecosystem functions
options.C: Only organic matter
options.D: Only water and air

questions.explanation: Soil is a dynamic natural body of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms supporting plant growth and ecosystem functions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: How is soil formed?

options.A: Only by volcanic eruptions
options.B: Through weathering of parent material and the addition, transformation and movement of organic and mineral materials under climate, organisms, relief and time
options.C: Only by river deposition
options.D: Only by human activity

questions.explanation: Soil forms through weathering of parent material and the addition, transformation and movement of organic and mineral materials influenced by climate, organisms, relief and time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are the five major soil-forming factors?

options.A: Sand, silt, clay, water and air
options.B: Parent material, climate, organisms, relief/topography and time
options.C: Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and sulphur
options.D: O, A, E, B and C horizons

questions.explanation: The five major soil-forming factors are parent material, climate, organisms, relief/topography and time.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 5

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is a soil profile?

options.A: A map of soil types in a district
options.B: A vertical section of soil showing its horizons from the surface downward to the parent material or bedrock
options.C: A list of soil nutrients
options.D: A method of soil testing

questions.explanation: A soil profile is a vertical section of soil showing its horizons from the surface downward to parent material or bedrock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are the main soil horizons?

options.A: A, B and C only
options.B: O, A, E, B, C and R horizons; not all soils contain every horizon
options.C: Topsoil and subsoil only
options.D: Sand, silt and clay

questions.explanation: Main horizons are O (organic), A (topsoil), E (evolution layer where present), B (subsoil/accumulation), C (weathered parent material) and R (bedrock); not every soil has all horizons.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 5

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is topsoil?

options.A: The bedrock layer
options.B: The upper mineral soil layer, commonly the A horizon, containing much of the soil's organic matter, biological activity and plant roots
options.C: The weathered parent material
options.D: The subsoil accumulation layer

questions.explanation: Topsoil is commonly the A horizon, containing much of the organic matter, biological activity and plant roots.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is alluvial soil?

options.A: Soil formed from river-deposited sediments, widespread in India's river plains and potentially productive
options.B: Soil formed from volcanic lava
options.C: Soil of arid regions with high salinity
options.D: Soil formed under intense leaching in humid climates

questions.explanation: Alluvial soil is formed from river-deposited sediments; it is widespread in India's river plains and can be productive, though fertility and texture vary.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is black soil?

options.A: Soil formed from river sediments
options.B: Clay-rich soil often associated with basaltic parent material in the Deccan region, with high moisture retention and cracks on drying
options.C: Soil with red colour from iron oxides
options.D: Soil of arid regions low in organic matter

questions.explanation: Black soil is clay-rich, often associated with basaltic parent material in the Deccan; many black soils have high moisture-retention capacity and develop cracks on drying.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 5

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is regur soil?

options.A: Another name for red soil
options.B: Another name commonly used for black cotton soil, especially in the Deccan region
options.C: Another name for laterite soil
options.D: Another name for alluvial soil

questions.explanation: Regur soil is another name commonly used for black cotton soil, especially in the Deccan region.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is red soil?

options.A: Soil whose red colour commonly results from iron oxides, widespread in parts of peninsular India
options.B: Soil formed from river sediments
options.C: Clay-rich soil associated with Deccan basalt
options.D: Soil of arid regions with salinity

questions.explanation: Red soil's red colour commonly results from iron oxides; it is widespread in parts of peninsular India and may be relatively low in organic matter and some nutrients.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is laterite soil?

options.A: Soil formed from river deposits
options.B: Soil formed under intense weathering and leaching in warm, humid climates, rich in iron and aluminium oxides
options.C: Soil of arid regions low in organic matter
options.D: Clay-rich soil associated with basaltic parent material

questions.explanation: Laterite soil forms under intense weathering and leaching in warm, humid climates; it can be rich in iron and aluminium oxides and may require careful nutrient management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is desert soil?

options.A: Soil of arid regions, often low in organic matter and moisture, with some areas having salinity or alkaline conditions
options.B: Soil formed under intense leaching in humid climates
options.C: Soil formed from river-deposited sediments
options.D: Clay-rich soil associated with Deccan basalt

questions.explanation: Desert soil occurs in arid regions, often low in organic matter and moisture; some areas have salinity or alkaline conditions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is mountain soil?

options.A: Soil formed from river deposits
options.B: A broad group of soils found in hilly and mountainous areas, varying greatly with altitude, slope, vegetation and parent material
options.C: Soil of arid regions with salinity
options.D: Clay-rich soil associated with basaltic parent material

questions.explanation: Mountain soil is a broad group found in hilly and mountainous areas, varying greatly with altitude, slope, vegetation and parent material.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: Which major soil groups occur in Karnataka?

options.A: Only black and red soils
options.B: Red, black, lateritic, alluvial and coastal sandy soils occur in different parts of Karnataka
options.C: Only alluvial and desert soils
options.D: Only lateritic and mountain soils

questions.explanation: Red, black, lateritic, alluvial and coastal sandy soils occur in different parts of Karnataka; local soil maps are more precise than broad labels.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is the idealised volumetric composition of a mineral soil?

options.A: About 45% mineral matter, 5% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air
options.B: About 25% mineral matter, 25% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air
options.C: About 50% mineral matter, 10% organic matter, 20% water and 20% air
options.D: About 60% mineral matter, 20% organic matter, 10% water and 10% air

questions.explanation: An idealised mineral soil by volume is often described as about 45% mineral matter, 5% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air, but actual proportions vary.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil texture?

options.A: The arrangement of soil particles into aggregates
options.B: The relative proportion of sand, silt and clay particles in soil
options.C: The capacity of soil to supply nutrients
options.D: The measure of soil acidity or alkalinity

questions.explanation: Soil texture is the relative proportion of sand, silt and clay particles in soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil structure?

options.A: The relative proportion of sand, silt and clay
options.B: The arrangement of soil particles into aggregates or pedes, affecting aeration, water movement, root growth and erosion resistance
options.C: The measure of soil pH
options.D: The capacity of soil to supply nutrients

questions.explanation: Soil structure is the arrangement of soil particles into aggregates or pedes, affecting aeration, water movement, root growth and erosion resistance.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil fertility?

options.A: The capacity of soil to supply essential nutrients in adequate amounts and suitable balance for plant growth
options.B: The capacity of soil to produce crops under a particular management system
options.C: The measure of soil acidity or alkalinity
options.D: The arrangement of soil particles into aggregates

questions.explanation: Soil fertility is the capacity of soil to supply essential nutrients in adequate amounts and suitable balance for plant growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil productivity?

options.A: The capacity of soil to supply essential nutrients only
options.B: The capacity of soil, under a particular management system and environment, to produce crops, depending on fertility and other physical, biological and climatic factors
options.C: The measure of soil acidity or alkalinity
options.D: The relative proportion of sand, silt and clay

questions.explanation: Soil productivity is the capacity of soil under a particular management system and environment to produce crops; it depends on fertility and other physical, biological and climatic factors.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil pH?

options.A: A measure of soil texture
options.B: A measure of soil acidity or alkalinity based on hydrogen-ion activity; pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline
options.C: A measure of soil organic matter
options.D: A measure of soil salinity

questions.explanation: Soil pH is a measure of acidity or alkalinity based on hydrogen-ion activity; pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 5

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: Why is soil pH important?

options.A: It only affects soil colour
options.B: It influences nutrient availability, microbial activity, toxicity of some elements and crop suitability
options.C: It only affects soil texture
options.D: It only affects soil water content

questions.explanation: Soil pH influences nutrient availability, microbial activity, toxicity of some elements and crop suitability.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are the primary plant nutrients?

options.A: Calcium, magnesium and sulphur
options.B: Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), commonly called the primary macronutrients
options.C: Iron, manganese and zinc
options.D: Boron, molybdenum and chlorine

questions.explanation: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are the primary plant nutrients, commonly called primary macronutrients.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 5

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are the secondary plant nutrients?

options.A: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
options.B: Calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S)
options.C: Iron, manganese and zinc
options.D: Copper, boron and molybdenum

questions.explanation: Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are the secondary plant nutrients.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 5

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are micronutrients?

options.A: Elements required in large amounts only
options.B: Elements required in small amounts, including iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel
options.C: Only nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
options.D: Only calcium, magnesium and sulphur

questions.explanation: Micronutrients are elements required in small amounts, including iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 6

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is nitrogen's role in plants?

options.A: It regulates osmotic balance and stomatal function
options.B: It is essential for amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll and supports vegetative growth
options.C: It is involved in energy transfer and root development
options.D: It is required only for seed formation

questions.explanation: Nitrogen is essential for amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll and supports vegetative growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is phosphorus's role in plants?

options.A: It supports vegetative growth only
options.B: It is involved in energy transfer (ATP), nucleic acids, membranes, root development, flowering and seed formation
options.C: It regulates stomatal function and water relations
options.D: It is essential for chlorophyll formation only

questions.explanation: Phosphorus is involved in energy transfer (ATP), nucleic acids, membranes, root development, flowering and seed formation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is potassium's role in plants?

options.A: It is essential for amino acids and proteins only
options.B: It regulates osmotic balance, stomatal function, enzyme activity, water relations and stress tolerance
options.C: It is involved in nucleic acid formation only
options.D: It supports only root development

questions.explanation: Potassium regulates osmotic balance, stomatal function, enzyme activity, water relations and stress tolerance.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil erosion?

options.A: The accumulation of salts in soil
options.B: Detachment and movement of soil by water, wind, ice or human activity, often removing nutrient-rich topsoil
options.C: The decline in soil organic matter
options.D: The compaction of soil by machinery

questions.explanation: Soil erosion is the detachment and movement of soil by water, wind, ice or human activity, often removing nutrient-rich topsoil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are the main types of water erosion?

options.A: Splash, sheet, rill, gully and stream-bank erosion
options.B: Wind, ice and glacial erosion only
options.C: Salinisation and alkalinisation
options.D: Compaction and waterlogging

questions.explanation: The main types of water erosion are splash, sheet, rill, gully and stream-bank erosion.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: How can soil erosion be controlled?

options.A: By removing all vegetation and deepening channels
options.B: By maintaining vegetative cover, contour farming, terracing, strip cropping, mulching, cover crops, shelterbelts, check dams and controlled grazing
options.C: By increasing tillage frequency only
options.D: By applying more chemical fertilisers

questions.explanation: Soil erosion can be controlled by maintaining vegetative cover, contour farming, terracing, strip cropping, mulching, cover crops, shelterbelts, check dams and controlled grazing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil conservation?

options.A: The protection and management of soil to prevent erosion, maintain fertility and preserve its physical, chemical and biological functions
options.B: The addition of chemical fertilisers to soil
options.C: The removal of topsoil for construction
options.D: The flooding of fields for irrigation

questions.explanation: Soil conservation is the protection and management of soil to prevent erosion, maintain fertility and preserve its physical, chemical and biological functions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil testing?

options.A: Laboratory or field analysis of soil samples to assess properties such as pH, electrical conductivity, organic carbon and available nutrients
options.B: The visual inspection of soil colour only
options.C: The measurement of soil temperature only
options.D: The counting of earthworms in soil

questions.explanation: Soil testing is laboratory or field analysis of soil samples to assess properties such as pH, electrical conductivity, organic carbon and available nutrients for informed nutrient management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: Why should soil samples be collected properly?

options.A: Because any sample gives the same result
options.B: Representative sampling at suitable depth and locations is essential; contaminated tools, unusual spots and poor mixing can produce misleading test results
options.C: Because soil testing requires only one sample from any spot
options.D: Because soil testing is not affected by sampling method

questions.explanation: Representative sampling at suitable depth and locations is essential; contaminated tools, unusual spots and poor mixing can produce misleading test results.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil salinity?

options.A: Excess accumulation of exchangeable sodium
options.B: Excess accumulation of soluble salts in soil, which can reduce plant water uptake, impair growth and lower crop yields
options.C: A decline in soil organic matter
options.D: The compaction of soil by machinery

questions.explanation: Soil salinity is the excess accumulation of soluble salts in soil, which can reduce plant water uptake, impair growth and lower crop yields.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil with excessive exchangeable sodium called?

options.A: Saline soil
options.B: Sodic soil, which can damage soil structure, reduce infiltration and restrict plant growth
options.C: Alluvial soil
options.D: Laterite soil

questions.explanation: Soil with excessive exchangeable sodium is sodic soil; it can damage soil structure, reduce infiltration and restrict plant growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil degradation?

options.A: The formation of soil from parent material
options.B: Decline in soil quality and functions due to erosion, salinisation, compaction, nutrient depletion, contamination, waterlogging or loss of organic matter
options.C: The addition of organic matter to soil
options.D: The testing of soil for nutrients

questions.explanation: Soil degradation is the decline in soil quality and functions due to erosion, salinisation, compaction, nutrient depletion, contamination, waterlogging or loss of organic matter.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is soil organic matter?

options.A: The decomposing and decomposed remains of plants, animals and microorganisms in soil
options.B: Only living plant roots
options.C: Only mineral particles
options.D: Only soil water

questions.explanation: Soil organic matter is the decomposing and decomposed remains of plants, animals and microorganisms in soil; it improves aggregation, water retention, nutrient cycling and biological activity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is compost?

options.A: A stable organic amendment produced by controlled decomposition of biodegradable materials under managed conditions
options.B: A chemical fertiliser containing NPK
options.C: A pesticide used to control soil pests
options.D: A type of irrigation water

questions.explanation: Compost is a stable organic amendment produced by controlled decomposition of biodegradable materials under managed conditions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is vermicompost?

options.A: Compost produced only by bacterial action
options.B: Organic manure produced through the activity of earthworms and associated microorganisms as they process organic residues
options.C: A chemical fertiliser containing only nitrogen
options.D: A type of green manure

questions.explanation: Vermicompost is organic manure produced through the activity of earthworms and associated microorganisms as they process organic residues.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What are the benefits of vermicompost?

options.A: It can improve soil structure, organic matter and nutrient availability; nutrient composition varies with feedstock and processing
options.B: It provides only nitrogen to plants
options.C: It completely replaces all fertilisers in all crops
options.D: It increases soil salinity

questions.explanation: Vermicompost can improve soil structure, organic matter and nutrient availability; nutrient composition varies with feedstock and processing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is green manuring?

options.A: Growing and incorporating green plant material into soil to add organic matter and nutrients, often using leguminous crops
options.B: Applying green-coloured chemical fertilisers
options.C: Growing crops only for sale
options.D: Using only vermicompost in fields

questions.explanation: Green manuring is growing and incorporating green plant material into soil to add organic matter and nutrients, often using leguminous crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Soil Science
questions.question: What is biochar?

options.A: A carbon-rich material produced by heating biomass under limited oxygen, sometimes used as a soil amendment after quality and suitability assessment
options.B: A chemical fertiliser containing potassium
options.C: A type of compost produced by earthworms
options.D: A pesticide made from plants

questions.explanation: Biochar is a carbon-rich material produced by heating biomass under limited oxygen and sometimes used as a soil amendment after quality and suitability assessment.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are cereals?

options.A: Grass-family crops grown mainly for their edible starchy grains, such as rice, wheat, maize, sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet
options.B: Dried edible seeds of leguminous crops
options.C: Crops grown for oil-rich seeds or fruits
options.D: Crops grown for fibres used in textiles

questions.explanation: Cereals are grass-family crops grown mainly for their edible starchy grains, such as rice, wheat, maize, sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are pulses?

options.A: Crops grown for fibres
options.B: Dried edible seeds of leguminous crops, such as chickpea, pigeon pea, lentil, mung bean, urad bean and peas; important sources of protein
options.C: Crops grown for oil-rich seeds
options.D: Grass-family crops grown for starchy grains

questions.explanation: Pulses are dried edible seeds of leguminous crops such as chickpea, pigeon pea, lentil, mung bean, urad bean and peas; they are important sources of protein.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are oilseed crops?

options.A: Crops grown for fibres
options.B: Crops grown for oil-rich seeds or fruits, such as groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame, safflower, castor and coconut
options.C: Grass-family crops grown for starchy grains
options.D: Dried edible seeds of leguminous crops

questions.explanation: Oilseed crops are grown for oil-rich seeds or fruits, such as groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame, safflower, castor and coconut.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are fibre crops?

options.A: Crops grown for oil-rich seeds
options.B: Crops grown for fibres used in textiles, ropes, paper or industry; examples include cotton, jute, mesta and sunn hemp
options.C: Grass-family crops grown for starchy grains
options.D: Dried edible seeds of leguminous crops

questions.explanation: Fibre crops are grown for fibres used in textiles, ropes, paper or industry; examples include cotton, jute, mesta and sunn hemp.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are cash crops in crop science?

options.A: Crops grown mainly for home consumption
options.B: Crops grown mainly for sale and income, such as cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, tea, coffee, rubber and some oilseeds
options.C: Crops grown only for animal feed
options.D: Crops grown only in Zaid season

questions.explanation: Cash crops are grown mainly for sale and income, such as cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, tea, coffee, rubber and some oilseeds.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are horticultural crops?

options.A: Only cereal crops
options.B: Crops including fruits, vegetables, flowers, plantation crops, spices, medicinal and aromatic plants and ornamental plants
options.C: Only pulses and oilseeds
options.D: Only fibre crops

questions.explanation: Horticultural crops include fruits, vegetables, flowers, plantation crops, spices, medicinal and aromatic plants and ornamental plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is pomology?

options.A: The branch of horticulture concerned with vegetable crops
options.B: The branch of horticulture concerned with fruit crops
options.C: The cultivation of flowers and ornamental plants
options.D: The cultivation of spices

questions.explanation: Pomology is the branch of horticulture concerned with fruit crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is olericulture?

options.A: The branch of horticulture concerned with fruit crops
options.B: The branch of horticulture concerned with vegetable crops
options.C: The cultivation of flowers and ornamental plants
options.D: The cultivation of spices

questions.explanation: Olericulture is the branch of horticulture concerned with vegetable crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is floriculture?

options.A: The cultivation and commercial production of flowers and ornamental plants
options.B: The cultivation of fruit crops
options.C: The cultivation of vegetable crops
options.D: The cultivation of medicinal plants

questions.explanation: Floriculture is the cultivation and commercial production of flowers and ornamental plants.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 6 and Page 11

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are spices?

options.A: Plant products used mainly for flavour, aroma or colour, such as pepper, cardamom, chilli, turmeric, ginger, coriander and cumin
options.B: Crops grown only for fibre
options.C: Dried edible seeds of leguminous crops
options.D: Grass-family crops grown for starchy grains

questions.explanation: Spices are plant products used mainly for flavour, aroma or colour, such as pepper, cardamom, chilli, turmeric, ginger, coriander and cumin.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What are medicinal plants?

options.A: Plants grown only for food
options.B: Plants containing substances used in traditional or modern healthcare and pharmaceutical research; safety and evidence vary by plant and preparation
options.C: Plants grown only for fibre
options.D: Plants grown only for ornamental purposes

questions.explanation: Medicinal plants contain substances used in traditional or modern healthcare and pharmaceutical research; safety and evidence vary by plant and preparation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is crop rotation?

options.A: Growing the same crop repeatedly on the same field
options.B: Growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same field over successive seasons or years to improve soil health, manage pests and use nutrients efficiently
options.C: Growing two or more crops together without row arrangement
options.D: Sowing a second crop before the first is harvested

questions.explanation: Crop rotation is growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same field over successive seasons or years to improve soil health, manage pests and use nutrients efficiently.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 7

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: Why are legumes included in crop rotations?

options.A: Because they cannot fix nitrogen
options.B: Because many legumes form symbioses with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which can contribute nitrogen to the farming system and diversify pest and nutrient cycles
options.C: Because they require no water
options.D: Because they are always cash crops

questions.explanation: Many legumes form symbioses with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which can contribute nitrogen to the farming system and diversify pest and nutrient cycles.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is multiple cropping?

options.A: Growing only one crop on the same land in a year
options.B: Growing more than one crop on the same land in a year, through sequential or simultaneous cropping
options.C: Growing crops only in the Rabi season
options.D: Growing crops without any irrigation

questions.explanation: Multiple cropping is growing more than one crop on the same land in a year, through sequential or simultaneous cropping.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is intercropping?

options.A: Growing two or more crops together without a distinct row arrangement
options.B: Growing two or more crops simultaneously in a definite row or spatial arrangement to use resources efficiently and reduce production risk
options.C: Sowing a second crop before the first is harvested
options.D: Growing different crops in a planned sequence over seasons

questions.explanation: Intercropping is growing two or more crops simultaneously in a definite row or spatial arrangement to use resources efficiently and reduce production risk.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 7

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is mixed cropping?

options.A: Growing two or more crops together on the same field without a distinct row arrangement, often as a risk-reduction strategy
options.B: Growing two or more crops simultaneously in a definite row arrangement
options.C: Growing different crops in a planned sequence over seasons
options.D: Sowing a second crop before the first is harvested

questions.explanation: Mixed cropping is growing two or more crops together on the same field without a distinct row arrangement, often as a risk-reduction strategy.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 7

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is the difference between intercropping and mixed cropping?

options.A: Intercropping uses a planned row or spatial pattern; mixed cropping generally involves less distinct arrangement and is often intended to reduce the risk of total crop failure
options.B: Intercropping involves no row arrangement; mixed cropping uses definite rows
options.C: Both are exactly the same practice
options.D: Intercropping is only for fruits; mixed cropping is only for cereals

questions.explanation: Intercropping uses a planned row or spatial pattern; mixed cropping generally involves less distinct arrangement and is often intended to reduce the risk of total crop failure.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is relay cropping?

options.A: Growing two or more crops together without row arrangement
options.B: Sowing a second crop before the first crop is harvested, so their growing periods overlap for a time
options.C: Growing different crops in a planned sequence over seasons
options.D: Growing only one crop in a year

questions.explanation: Relay cropping is sowing a second crop before the first crop is harvested, so their growing periods overlap for a time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is a high-yielding variety (HYV)?

options.A: A crop variety selected or bred for high yield potential under suitable management and environmental conditions
options.B: A variety that yields poorly but resists all pests
options.C: A variety grown only without irrigation
options.D: A variety grown only in organic farming

questions.explanation: A high-yielding variety is a crop variety selected or bred for high yield potential under suitable management and environmental conditions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is a hybrid seed?

options.A: Seed produced by crossing selected parent lines to obtain first-generation (F1) plants that may show hybrid vigour or uniformity
options.B: Seed produced by self-pollination over many generations
options.C: Seed collected from wild plants
options.D: Seed produced without any crossing

questions.explanation: A hybrid seed is produced by crossing selected parent lines to obtain first-generation (F1) plants that may show hybrid vigour or uniformity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: Can farmers reliably save seed from all F1 hybrids for the next crop?

options.A: Yes, F1 hybrids always breed true in the next generation
options.B: Not generally; the next generation may segregate and lose the uniform performance of the F1
options.C: Yes, but only for cereal crops
options.D: Yes, but only for pulse crops

questions.explanation: Not generally. The next generation may segregate and lose the uniform performance of the F1; seed choice depends on crop and variety type.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is seed treatment?

options.A: Application of physical, chemical or biological agents to seed before sowing to protect against seed- and soil-borne pests or improve establishment
options.B: The storage of seed after harvest
options.C: The harvesting of seed from the field
options.D: The certification of seed by an agency

questions.explanation: Seed treatment is the application of physical, chemical or biological agents to seed before sowing to protect against seed- and soil-borne pests or improve establishment.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is seed viability?

options.A: The ability of a seed to remain alive and germinate under suitable conditions
options.B: The size of the seed
options.C: The colour of the seed
options.D: The weight of the seed

questions.explanation: Seed viability is the ability of a seed to remain alive and germinate under suitable conditions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is seed dormancy?

options.A: The ability of a seed to germinate immediately after harvest
options.B: A condition in which a viable seed does not germinate even under otherwise favourable conditions until specific requirements are met
options.C: The death of a seed
options.D: The certification of a seed

questions.explanation: Seed dormancy is a condition in which a viable seed does not germinate even under otherwise favourable conditions until specific requirements are met.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is seed storage?

options.A: Maintaining seed quality and viability under suitable moisture, temperature, hygiene and packaging conditions
options.B: The sowing of seed in the field
options.C: The harvesting of seed from the field
options.D: The certification of seed by an agency

questions.explanation: Seed storage is maintaining seed quality and viability under suitable moisture, temperature, hygiene and packaging conditions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is seed certification?

options.A: A regulated process to maintain and verify seed identity, genetic purity, physical quality and germination standards
options.B: The storage of seed after harvest
options.C: The sowing of seed in the field
options.D: The harvesting of seed from the field

questions.explanation: Seed certification is a regulated process to maintain and verify seed identity, genetic purity, physical quality and germination standards.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is harvesting?

options.A: The process of collecting a mature crop or its economic produce from the field at an appropriate stage
options.B: The separation of grain from stalks
options.C: The separation of grain from chaff using air
options.D: The storage of produce after harvest

questions.explanation: Harvesting is the process of collecting a mature crop or its economic produce from the field at an appropriate stage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: Why is correct harvesting time important?

options.A: Harvesting too early or late can reduce yield, quality, storage life and market value and may increase field losses
options.B: Harvesting time has no effect on yield or quality
options.C: Harvesting early always improves storage life
options.D: Harvesting late always increases market value

questions.explanation: Harvesting too early or late can reduce yield, quality, storage life and market value and may increase field losses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is threshing?

options.A: Separation of grain or seeds from harvested stalks, pods or panicles
options.B: Separation of grain from lighter chaff using air movement
options.C: The collection of a mature crop from the field
options.D: The storage of produce after harvest

questions.explanation: Threshing is the separation of grain or seeds from harvested stalks, pods or panicles.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is winnowing?

options.A: Separation of grain or seeds from harvested stalks
options.B: Separation of grain from lighter chaff using air movement
options.C: The collection of a mature crop from the field
options.D: The storage of produce after harvest

questions.explanation: Winnowing is the separation of grain from lighter chaff using air movement.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is post-harvest management?

options.A: Handling, drying, cleaning, grading, storage, processing, packaging and transport of produce to minimise losses and maintain quality
options.B: The sowing of seed in the field
options.C: The application of fertilisers to crops
options.D: The irrigation of crops in the field

questions.explanation: Post-harvest management includes handling, drying, cleaning, grading, storage, processing, packaging and transport of produce to minimise losses and maintain quality.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Crop Science
questions.question: What is crop diversification?

options.A: Shifting from a narrow set of crops to a broader range of crops or enterprises to improve resilience, income opportunities and resource use
options.B: Growing only one crop repeatedly
options.C: Growing crops only in the Kharif season
options.D: Growing crops only without irrigation

questions.explanation: Crop diversification is shifting from a narrow set of crops to a broader range of crops or enterprises to improve resilience, income opportunities and resource use.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is irrigation?

options.A: Artificial application of water to crops when rainfall is insufficient or poorly distributed
options.B: The natural fall of rain on crops
options.C: The drainage of excess water from fields
options.D: The storage of water in reservoirs

questions.explanation: Irrigation is the artificial application of water to crops when rainfall is insufficient or poorly distributed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is surface irrigation?

options.A: Water is sprayed through pressurized pipes and nozzles
options.B: Water is conveyed over the soil surface by gravity, using methods such as basin, border and furrow irrigation
options.C: Water is delivered slowly near plant roots through emitters
options.D: Water is applied through a controlled greenhouse system

questions.explanation: Surface irrigation conveys water over the soil surface by gravity, using methods such as basin, border and furrow irrigation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is basin irrigation?

options.A: A surface-irrigation method in which a field or tree basin is surrounded by bunds and filled with water
options.B: Water flows through small channels between crop rows
options.C: Water is sprayed through nozzles to simulate rainfall
options.D: Water is delivered through emitters near roots

questions.explanation: Basin irrigation is a surface-irrigation method in which a field or tree basin is surrounded by bunds and filled with water.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is furrow irrigation?

options.A: A method in which a basin is surrounded by bunds and filled with water
options.B: Water flows through small channels between crop rows and infiltrates into the root zone
options.C: Water is sprayed through pressurized nozzles
options.D: Water is delivered slowly through emitters

questions.explanation: Furrow irrigation lets water flow through small channels between crop rows and infiltrate into the root zone.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is sprinkler irrigation?

options.A: Water is delivered slowly near plant roots through emitters
options.B: Water is sprayed through pressurized pipes and nozzles to simulate rainfall over the crop or soil surface
options.C: Water flows through small channels between crop rows
options.D: Water is conveyed over the soil surface by gravity

questions.explanation: Sprinkler irrigation sprays water through pressurized pipes and nozzles to simulate rainfall over the crop or soil surface.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 7

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is drip irrigation?

options.A: Water is sprayed through nozzles to simulate rainfall
options.B: Water is delivered slowly and locally near plant roots through emitters, reducing evaporation and often improving water-use efficiency
options.C: Water flows over the soil surface by gravity
options.D: Water is stored in a reservoir for later use

questions.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water slowly and locally near plant roots through emitters, reducing evaporation and often improving water-use efficiency.
questions.source: Agricultural Science Study Guide, Page 3 and Page 7

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is micro-irrigation?

options.A: A category including drip and micro-sprinkler systems that apply water in controlled quantities near the crop root zone
options.B: Flooding the entire field with water
options.C: Applying water only through canals
options.D: Applying water only through wells

questions.explanation: Micro-irrigation is a category including drip and micro-sprinkler systems that apply water in controlled quantities near the crop root zone.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What are the advantages of drip irrigation?

options.A: It can reduce water losses, limit weed growth between rows, support fertigation and improve water-use efficiency, but requires filtration, maintenance and suitable design
options.B: It requires no maintenance and no filtration
options.C: It always increases evaporation losses
options.D: It is suitable for all crops without any design considerations

questions.explanation: Drip irrigation can reduce water losses, limit weed growth between rows, support fertigation and improve water-use efficiency, but requires filtration, maintenance and suitable design.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What are the limitations of sprinkler irrigation?

options.A: It has no limitations
options.B: Wind, evaporation, energy costs, nozzle clogging and water quality can reduce performance; some crops and soils are less suitable
options.C: It can only be used in greenhouses
options.D: It requires no energy

questions.explanation: Wind, evaporation, energy costs, nozzle clogging and water quality can reduce sprinkler performance; some crops and soils are less suitable.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is fertigation?

options.A: Application of dissolved fertilizers through an irrigation system, commonly drip irrigation
options.B: Application of fertilizers by hand to the soil
options.C: Application of water through canals
options.D: Application of pesticides through sprayers

questions.explanation: Fertigation is the application of dissolved fertilizers through an irrigation system, commonly drip irrigation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is water-use efficiency in agriculture?

options.A: The total amount of water supplied to a field
options.B: The amount of crop output or biomass produced per unit of water supplied or consumed; the exact measure depends on the definition used
options.C: The total rainfall received in a year
options.D: The storage capacity of an irrigation tank

questions.explanation: Water-use efficiency is the amount of crop output or biomass produced per unit of water supplied or consumed; the exact measure depends on the definition used.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is watershed management?

options.A: Integrated planning and management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage basin to conserve soil and water and improve livelihoods
options.B: The construction of canals only
options.C: The drilling of tube wells only
options.D: The application of fertilizers through drip irrigation

questions.explanation: Watershed management is integrated planning and management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage basin to conserve soil and water and improve livelihoods.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is farm mechanisation?

options.A: Use of machinery and equipment to perform farm operations such as land preparation, sowing, irrigation, harvesting and post-harvest handling
options.B: Use of only manual labour for farm operations
options.C: Use of only animal power for farm operations
options.D: Use of only chemical inputs in farming

questions.explanation: Farm mechanisation is the use of machinery and equipment to perform farm operations such as land preparation, sowing, irrigation, harvesting and post-harvest handling.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is a tractor?

options.A: A powered farm vehicle used to pull or operate implements and machinery for agricultural and related work
options.B: A machine that combines reaping, threshing and winnowing
options.C: A machine that places seeds at controlled depth and spacing
options.D: A machine that places nursery-raised seedlings into the field

questions.explanation: A tractor is a powered farm vehicle used to pull or operate implements and machinery for agricultural and related work.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is a combine harvester?

options.A: A machine that combines reaping, threshing and winnowing/cleaning operations to harvest grain crops
options.B: A machine that places seeds at controlled depth and spacing
options.C: A machine that places nursery-raised seedlings into the field
options.D: A powered farm vehicle used to pull implements

questions.explanation: A combine harvester combines reaping, threshing and winnowing/cleaning operations to harvest grain crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: Which of the following are common agricultural machines?

options.A: Ploughs, harrows, seed drills, planters, cultivators, sprayers, weeders, threshers, combine harvesters, balers and irrigation pumps
options.B: Only tractors and combine harvesters
options.C: Only sprayers and threshers
options.D: Only seed drills and planters

questions.explanation: Common agricultural machines include ploughs, harrows, seed drills, planters, cultivators, sprayers, weeders, threshers, combine harvesters, balers and irrigation pumps.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is precision agriculture?

options.A: Site-specific crop and resource management using data, sensors, positioning systems, imagery and digital tools to apply inputs where and when needed
options.B: Growing crops without any technology
options.C: Applying the same inputs uniformly across the entire field regardless of variability
options.D: Farming only in controlled greenhouses

questions.explanation: Precision agriculture is site-specific crop and resource management using data, sensors, positioning systems, imagery and digital tools to apply inputs where and when needed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is smart farming?

options.A: Use of connected sensors, automation, data analytics, AI, robotics and digital platforms to monitor and manage farm operations
options.B: Farming without any technology
options.C: Applying the same inputs uniformly across the entire field
options.D: Farming only in controlled greenhouses

questions.explanation: Smart farming uses connected sensors, automation, data analytics, AI, robotics and digital platforms to monitor and manage farm operations.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: How is remote sensing used in agriculture?

options.A: Satellite and aerial imagery can help assess crop area, crop health, soil moisture, drought, irrigation, pest stress and damage after disasters
options.B: It is used only for weather forecasting
options.C: It is used only for soil testing in laboratories
options.D: It is used only for harvesting crops

questions.explanation: Satellite and aerial imagery can help assess crop area, crop health, soil moisture, drought, irrigation, pest stress and damage after disasters.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: How are drones used in agriculture?

options.A: Drones can map fields, monitor crop health, survey damage and where legally permitted and safely operated, apply selected agricultural inputs
options.B: Drones are used only for entertainment
options.C: Drones are used only for harvesting crops
options.D: Drones are used only for soil testing

questions.explanation: Drones can map fields, monitor crop health, survey damage and where legally permitted and safely operated, apply selected agricultural inputs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What are soil sensors?

options.A: Devices that measure properties such as soil moisture, temperature, electrical conductivity or nutrient-related indicators to support irrigation and crop management
options.B: Devices used only for measuring rainfall
options.C: Devices used only for measuring wind speed
options.D: Devices used only for measuring sunlight

questions.explanation: Soil sensors measure properties such as soil moisture, temperature, electrical conductivity or nutrient-related indicators to support irrigation and crop management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is agricultural biotechnology?

options.A: Use of biological and molecular methods for crop improvement, diagnostics, tissue culture, biofertilisers, biopesticides and stress-resilient varieties
options.B: Use of only chemical fertilisers in farming
options.C: Use of only traditional farming methods
options.D: Use of only irrigation technologies

questions.explanation: Agricultural biotechnology uses biological and molecular methods for crop improvement, diagnostics, tissue culture, biofertilisers, biopesticides and stress-resilient varieties.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is a seed drill?

options.A: A machine that places seeds at controlled depth and spacing and often covers them with soil
options.B: A machine that combines reaping, threshing and winnowing
options.C: A machine that places nursery-raised seedlings into the field
options.D: A powered farm vehicle used to pull implements

questions.explanation: A seed drill places seeds at controlled depth and spacing and often covers them with soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is a transplanter?

options.A: A machine that places seeds at controlled depth and spacing
options.B: A machine that places nursery-raised seedlings into the field at planned spacing and depth
options.C: A machine that combines reaping, threshing and winnowing
options.D: A powered farm vehicle used to pull implements

questions.explanation: A transplanter places nursery-raised seedlings into the field at planned spacing and depth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is a controlled-environment greenhouse?

options.A: A protected cultivation structure in which temperature, humidity, light, ventilation and sometimes CO2 are managed to improve crop production
options.B: An open field used for crop production
options.C: A storage structure for harvested produce
options.D: A structure used only for livestock housing

questions.explanation: A controlled-environment greenhouse is a protected cultivation structure in which temperature, humidity, light, ventilation and sometimes CO2 are managed to improve crop production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is fertigation's main benefit?

options.A: It can synchronise nutrient delivery with crop water needs and growth stages, but requires correct nutrient compatibility and system maintenance
options.B: It eliminates the need for any irrigation
options.C: It always increases water losses
options.D: It requires no system maintenance

questions.explanation: Fertigation can synchronise nutrient delivery with crop water needs and growth stages, but requires correct nutrient compatibility and system maintenance.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Irrigation and Agricultural Technology
questions.question: What is a farm management information system?

options.A: A digital system that records and analyses farm activities, inputs, costs, yields, inventory, weather and market information
options.B: A system used only for irrigation scheduling
options.C: A system used only for livestock breeding
options.D: A system used only for soil testing

questions.explanation: A farm management information system records and analyses farm activities, inputs, costs, yields, inventory, weather and market information.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Plant Protection
questions.question: What is plant protection?

options.A: The prevention, monitoring and management of diseases, insect pests, weeds and other factors that reduce crop health and yield
options.B: The application of fertilisers to crops
options.C: The irrigation of crops
options.D: The harvesting of crops

questions.explanation: Plant protection is the prevention, monitoring and management of diseases, insect pests, weeds and other factors that reduce crop health and yield.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Plant Protection
questions.question: What is a plant disease?

options.A: A harmful disturbance of normal plant structure or function caused by pathogens or non-infectious environmental factors
options.B: The normal growth of a plant
options.C: The application of fertilisers to a plant
options.D: The harvesting of a plant

questions.explanation: A plant disease is a harmful disturbance of normal plant structure or function caused by pathogens or non-infectious environmental factors.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Plant Protection
questions.question: What are the major groups of plant pathogens?

options.A: Only fungi and bacteria
options.B: Fungi, bacteria, viruses, viroids, phytoplasmas, nematodes and some parasitic plants
options.C: Only viruses and nematodes
options.D: Only fungi and parasitic plants

questions.explanation: Major groups of plant pathogens include fungi, bacteria, viruses, viroids, phytoplasmas, nematodes and some parasitic plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.topic: Plant Protection
questions.question: What is a fungal plant disease?

options.A: A disease caused by a fungus or fungus-like organism; examples include rusts, smuts, powdery mildew, downy mildew and many rots
options.B: A disease caused by a virus
options.C: A disease caused by a bacterium
